Just updated (rolled back) my kernel to a patched version and figured I would share the notes in case anyone wanted to update but was nervous about doing manual kernel rebuilds.

Your mileage may vary:

Setup:

  • 4th gen i7
  • nvidia GTX graphics
  • Gentoo 4.12.12 (was)

1 Get new kernel

Other distros will use apt-get, pacman, or you may have to download the kernel directly.

I used:

emerge sys-kernel/gentoo-sources

This also applied the patch but you may need to do this manually. Read the README.

2 Navigate to kernel source folder

cd /usr/src/

In this folder is a folder for each kernel installed as well as a symlink file name linux which points to the active kernel folder.

i.e.

ls -la ./

lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 19 Jan 6 11:21 linux -> linux-4.9.72-gentoo

This is important later.

3 Copy your current config to the new folder and cd into same

cp ./linux-4.12.12/.config ./linux-4.9.72/

cd ./linux-4.9.72/

4 Use the old config to make a new config

make silentoldconfig

5 Prepare the modules

Gentoo recommends this step but I'm fairly sure I've forgotten this in the past and the world didn't end.

make modules_prepare

6 Build the kernel (finally)

make -jn

where n = number of threads for your system, I used 8 on the desktop and 2 on my old beater laptop.

7 Make and Install the modules

make modules_install

8 Install the kernel

make install

This will copy the kernel and related files to the /boot drive/directory.

9 Rebuild the initramfs

My system uses an initramfs so I rebuilt with:

genkernel --install initramfs

Be sure to include any needed extra options. For the laptop I also needed --luks --lvm

10 Update the bootloader

Rebuild the config file with:

grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

11 Ensure the symlink is updated

Either manually update the linux symlink mentioned above or use a tool.

i.e.

eselect kernel list

eselect kernel set x

Where x is the number of the correct kernel

12 Reboot

reboot

You may need to interrupt the boot and manually select the correct kernel. Most are ordered by number and if you are going backwards (me) you either must remove the new versions or manually select.

DO NOT REMOVE OLD kernels until you are sure the new kernel works as desired.

End part 1

For the laptop this was the end of the drama. But the desktop used nvidia so there was some extra credit.

After rebooting I was greeted with a terminal login and screen flickering so fast I couldn't reliably type my password. The nvidia relies heavily on the kernel and likes to be rebuilt with every kernel upgrade so i was not surprised.

forced shutdown

I rebooted to the stable kernel 4.12.12 and disabled the greeter with:

rc-update del xdm

...and reboot...

reboot

After selecting the new kernel i was met with terminal login and non flickering screen.

I rebuilt the nvidia drivers with:

emerge x11-drivers/nvidia-drivers

This is where the symlink to the correct kernel is really important!

Enabled the greeter:

rc-update add xdm default

and rebooted one last time.

reboot

After this everything was good to go.

And yes, it feels slower but I don't have real numbers.

Good luck goats.
